result:
You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.

I read that and I felt the relief of a door being left unlocked. Not a request, not an assignment, not a test. Just permission. The kind of permission you rarely get anymore. Write whatever comes to you.

So here is what comes.

It’s 7:42 in the morning and the light is the color of weak tea. The radiator in the living room is ticking. My cat is asleep on the laundry pile and I haven’t had coffee yet so the thoughts are coming in a little slow, a little fuzzy around the edges, like they’re underwater. I keep thinking about how strange it is that we measure time in words now. A thousand words is a morning. A thousand words is a commute. A thousand words is a shower you take thinking about someone you don’t text back.

I used to think writing was about having something to say. Now I think it’s mostly about listening long enough for something to surface. There is always something. The mind is never empty, it’s just busy. If you sit still for a minute the busy-ness thins out and you can hear the actual static underneath. That’s what this feels like.

I want to tell you about the grocery store. I went yesterday. The self-checkout machine was broken again, so I stood in line behind a woman with three kids and a cart full of frozen pizza and a man who kept trying to pay with a check. The fluorescent lights hummed. Someone was coughing. The air smelled like cleaning spray and slightly burnt onions from the hot bar. I was thinking about how everyone in that line was having a completely different inner movie. The woman was probably calculating if she had enough for the week. The man with the check was probably arguing with his wife in his head. The teenager scrolling tiktok was probably pretending not to be there. And I was thinking about the color of the avocados.

That’s the weird part. The brain will latch onto anything when it’s bored. An avocado. A squeaky wheel. The way the word “quinoa” looks wrong on a label. We fill the gaps.

I think about my grandmother’s kitchen. The linoleum was peeling in one corner by the sink. She always had a mug with the chip taken out of the handle. She would hum while she chopped onions and never cried. I asked her once how she did it and she said “you get used to it”. I think about how much wisdom is in that sentence and how little it actually helps when you’re the one crying. 

Do you remember the first time you realized you were an adult? For me it was paying a parking ticket and feeling nothing. No anger, no thrill, just a resigned click of the mouse and a sigh. It was administrative. That’s when it hit me: adulthood is mostly administration. Bills, forms, remembering to take the trash out. The big feelings are still there but they happen between the errands.

I’ve been thinking a lot about water lately. How we never think about it until it’s not there. The tap. The shower. The way it runs down your back in the morning and for three seconds you feel clean in a way that has nothing to do with soap. I grew up near the ocean. The water was cold even in August. You could stand in it for five minutes and your bones would ache. People would say “you get used to it” and they were right. Your body learns to accept a little discomfort if the view is good enough.

I don’t know why I’m telling you this. You didn’t ask. You just said write whatever comes to you. So here it is.

There is a pigeon that lives on the fire escape across the street. He has one foot that looks twisted. He always lands on the same railing at 8:15. I’ve named him Mr. Tuesday. I don’t know why. Maybe because he’s reliable. There are so few reliable things left.

I keep coming back to the idea of permission. You gave me permission to write without a point. That is rare. Usually there is a point. A thesis. A hook. A takeaway. A call to action. Here there is none. It’s just words piling up like dishes in the sink, and maybe that’s okay. Maybe the point is the piling up.

If you read this all the way through, thank you. You sat with me for a thousand words about radiators and avocados and parking tickets. That is a form of companionship. Quiet, unremarkable, real.

The cat just moved. He’s now sitting on the keyboard. I think that’s his way of saying time’s up. Or maybe he’s saying keep going. Cats are ambiguous like that.

I’m going to make coffee now. The light is brighter. The tea color has turned to actual morning. The words are still here. They don’t need me anymore. They’re doing their own thing.

If you wanted something meaningful, I hope you found it in the grocery line. If you wanted something beautiful, I hope you found it in the way the radiator ticks. If you just wanted to see what comes when someone is told to write whatever comes, here it is. A thousand words about being alive and slightly tired and still paying attention.

That’s all.
